In January she took it out again and put it in a tin that had once held boiled sweets, on the shelf above the stove, where by then there were thirty of its fellows. She had never opened one. The village had its theories, because the village always did. Mrs. Prell at the shop held that Ottilie had been sweet on Bryn Cadoc since before the war and could not bear to see his letters go to a woman in Tarne. The schoolmaster, who was fond of a grievance, held that the Havering office had been slovenly for years and that a letter went astray there most winters. Ottilie's own sister held that it was kindness: that Ilse Mawer had been ill a long time and did not need a letter every December from a man who had gone away in 1961 and not come back.

None of the three had been in the sorting room on the morning Bryn Cadoc came in with his coat still wet and set the first of them on the counter. He did not ask her to post it. She said that it was what she had said.

Between 1908 and 1931 the Farne Institute bought two hundred and six plaster casts of classical heads for its teaching collection, and entered every one of them in the register as the work of the Bramm workshop in Leipzig. Bramm's name was a guarantee. The firm took its moulds from the marbles themselves, under licence, in Rome and Naples and Munich, and its casts were bought by schools that could not send their pupils to see the originals.

In 1994 Imre Vass set out to check the register, and the instrument he used was shrinkage. Plaster taken from a mould comes out very slightly smaller than the thing the mould was taken from; a cast made from a mould taken off another cast is smaller again, by about the same fraction a second time. The difference is under a millimetre across a human head, but it is consistent, and Vass had the published measurements of the marbles to compare against. He measured the same three dimensions on every one of the two hundred and six.

The figures fell into two groups. A hundred and forty-five sat where a first cast should sit. Sixty-one sat a further step down, and they answer to one another closely but not to the rest. Vass then did the thing the register made easy: he looked up when each of the sixty-one had come in. Every one of them had been bought between 1919 and 1923, and no cast bought in those five years fell into the other group.

Bramm's own papers explain what the Institute could not have known. The firm's moulding shop was under water in the winter of 1918 and out of use for four years, and its printed catalogue for 1920 is the largest it ever issued. A workshop that is selling more heads than it can mould must be getting them from somewhere, and the somewhere leaves its mark in the plaster.

The Institute was told once. The minutes of the Standing Committee for March 1923 record a curator's complaint that the new heads “do not take the light as the older ones do, being softer in the feature”. The complaint was minuted, thanked, and not acted upon, and it is the only contemporary notice of a difference that anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers at any time in the seventy years that followed. Vass says so twice.
